document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 42-year-old fair-skinned woman describes 2 years of episodic facial flushing triggered by hot drinks, alcohol, and spicy food. Examination shows persistent non-transient erythema with fine telangiectasia and scattered dome-shaped inflammatory papules and pustules over the cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead. No comedones are present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes rosacea as dome-shaped inflammatory papules with or without pustules, accompanied by flushing, non-transient erythema, and telangiectasia, distributed typically over the central face including forehead, nose, cheeks, and chin, with exacerbating factors including heat, sun, stress, hot liquids, alcohol, and spices. It is most prevalent in fair-skinned people aged 30-50 and is more common in women.

optionExplanations.b: Acne vulgaris is characterised by comedones and involves the neck, upper chest, and back as well as the face.
optionExplanations.c: Perioral dermatitis produces papulopustules confined to perioral, perinasal, or periorbital skin with a rim of sparing around the vermillion border.
optionExplanations.d: Seborrheic dermatitis produces greasy scale rather than flushing with telangiectasia and inflammatory papules.
optionExplanations.e: Contact dermatitis presents as poorly demarcated erythematous eczematous plaques, not flushing with telangiectasia.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man reports 4 days of burning pain and paresthesia across his right mid-back, followed 3 days ago by an eruption. Examination shows grouped vesicles, bullae, and pustules on an erythematous, edematous base confined to a single thoracic dermatome on the right, not crossing the midline. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral valacyclovir for 7 days plus analgesia
Potent topical corticosteroid applied twice daily

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes herpes zoster as a unilateral dermatomal eruption occurring 3-5 days after pain and paresthesia of that dermatome, with vesicles, bullae, and pustules on an erythematous edematous base, and notes that lesions rarely cross the midline. Management is oral antivirals (famciclovir, valacyclovir, or acyclovir) for 7 days, which must be initiated within 72 hours to be of benefit, together with analgesia and saline or Burow's compresses.

optionExplanations.b: Antibacterials do not treat reactivation of varicella zoster virus.
optionExplanations.c: Topical corticosteroids are not the treatment for an acute dermatomal zoster eruption.
optionExplanations.d: Shingrix is used for prevention in people over 50, not as treatment of an active eruption.
optionExplanations.e: Terbinafine is an antifungal used for dermatophyte infections such as tinea capitis and onychomycosis.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl has an 18-month history of intensely pruritic rash. Examination shows poorly demarcated erythematous plaques with scaling and excoriations in the antecubital and popliteal flexures, with lichenification of the wrists and generalized xerosis. Her palms show marked hyperlinearity. She has asthma and her mother has allergic rhinitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines atopic dermatitis as a subacute and chronic eczematous reaction with prolonged severe pruritus, in which inflammation, lichenification, and excoriations are secondary to relentless scratching, and describes atopic palms with hyperlinearity, associated xerosis and keratosis pilaris, and an age-dependent distribution. It affects 10-20% of children under 5 in developed countries and is associated with a personal or family history of atopy such as asthma or allergic rhinitis.

optionExplanations.b: Asteatotic dermatitis is a mild pruritic dermatitis of dry skin that is very common in the elderly, predominating on the shins with a dried river bed appearance.
optionExplanations.c: Psoriasis produces well-circumscribed plaques with silvery-white scale on extensor surfaces, the opposite distribution to flexural atopic dermatitis.
optionExplanations.d: Tinea corporis is a scaly round or oval plaque with an active erythematous margin and central clearing.
optionExplanations.e: Pityriasis rosea is an acute self-limiting eruption of oval plaques with central scale following skin tension lines after a herald patch.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy with known atopic dermatitis has a 1-week flare with intensely itchy, poorly demarcated erythematous scaling plaques on both antecubital fossae. There is no crusting, purulence, or fever. He uses a fragrance-free emollient daily and avoids known irritants. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic therapy for this flare?

options.text: Topical corticosteroid of appropriate potency applied twice daily for at least 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes places acute control of an atopic dermatitis flare with topical corticosteroids or a topical calcineurin inhibitor, layered on top of daily emollients and trigger avoidance. Topical corticosteroids are effective in reducing acute flares, with potency chosen according to age, body site, and duration of use, applied as one adult fingertip unit per two adult palms of skin twice daily for at least 2 weeks.

optionExplanations.b: Oral steroids sit at the severe refractory end of the treatment algorithm, not first line for a localized flare.
optionExplanations.c: Oral antibiotics such as cephalexin are for widespread S. aureus superinfection, and there is no crusting or purulence here.
optionExplanations.d: Dupilumab is a biologic reserved for severe refractory disease.
optionExplanations.e: Phototherapy is also reserved for severe refractory disease rather than an initial localized flare.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman has 3 months of an itchy eruption. Examination shows symmetrical, bilateral, well-demarcated violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules and plaques on the flexor wrists and shins. Inside the mouth there is a lacy whitish reticular network on the buccal mucosa. Some lesions have appeared along a recent scratch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes lichen planus as pruritic, well-demarcated, violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules and plaques distributed symmetrically and bilaterally, with common sites at the wrists, nails, scalp, and mucous membranes in 60% of cases. Wickham's striae, a lacy whitish reticular network mostly on oral mucosa, are pathognomonic, and the Koebner phenomenon accounts for lesions arising along a scratch.

optionExplanations.b: Psoriasis produces erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale on extensor surfaces, with Auspitz sign rather than Wickham's striae.
optionExplanations.c: Pityriasis rosea consists of oval plaques with central scale along skin tension lines preceded by a herald patch.
optionExplanations.d: Nummular dermatitis produces coin-shaped eczematous plaques without violaceous polygonal papules or oral striae.
optionExplanations.e: Secondary syphilis is in the differential of papulosquamous disease but does not produce Wickham's striae or the 6P morphology.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man reports that a single 3 cm oval scaly plaque appeared on his flank 10 days ago. Over the past 3 days multiple smaller red oval plaques with central scale that does not extend to the edge of the lesion have erupted on his trunk and proximal arms, with their long axes running parallel to the ribs. He feels well and is mildly itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes characterises pityriasis rosea as an acute, self-limiting eruption of red or flesh-coloured oval plaques with central scale that does not extend to the edge of the lesion, whose long axes follow skin tension lines parallel to the ribs, producing the Christmas tree pattern on the back. Most cases begin with a herald patch preceding other lesions by 1-2 weeks, and the trunk and proximal arms and legs are the usual sites.

optionExplanations.b: Guttate psoriasis produces droplet-like plaques with silvery scale and is not preceded by a herald patch.
optionExplanations.c: Tinea corporis is a pruritic scaly plaque with an active erythematous margin and central clearing, usually solitary or few in number.
optionExplanations.d: Lichen planus consists of violaceous polygonal flat-topped papules, characteristically on the wrists and mucous membranes.
optionExplanations.e: Nummular dermatitis produces coin-shaped eczematous plaques that do not follow Langer lines or begin with a herald patch.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man has well-circumscribed erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale on both elbows, both knees, and the scalp. Removing the scale produces pinpoint bleeding. The plaques involve about 2% of his body surface area and worsen each winter. He has no joint symptoms. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Topical corticosteroid with or without a topical vitamin D analogue

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes plaque psoriasis as well-circumscribed erythematous papules and plaques with silvery-white scales on the scalp, extensor elbows and knees, and trunk, with the Auspitz sign of pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed and worsening in winter. Management depends on severity: for mild disease with body surface area under 3%, first line treatment is a topical corticosteroid with or without a topical vitamin D analogue combination.

optionExplanations.b: Methotrexate is a systemic option for moderate to severe disease, not for 2% body surface area involvement.
optionExplanations.c: Acitretin is a systemic retinoid used for severe psoriasis and is teratogenic and hepatotoxic.
optionExplanations.d: PUVA is reserved for more extensive disease and carries lifetime session limits because of skin cancer risk.
optionExplanations.e: Cyclosporine is a systemic agent used for intermittent control in more severe disease and carries renal toxicity.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman has 6 weeks of intense pruritus followed by blistering. Examination shows large tense bullae on an erythematous base over the flexor forearms, axillae, medial thighs, and lower abdomen, with some urticarial plaques and no bullae in between. The oral mucosa is clear and shear stress on normal skin does not produce detachment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines bullous pemphigoid as a chronic autoimmune bullous eruption of pruritic, tense, subepidermal bullae on an erythematous or normal skin base, which may also present as urticarial plaques without bullae, at the flexor forearms, axillae, medial thighs, groin, and abdomen, with a mean age of onset of 60-80 years. The memory aid is that pemphigoiD lesions are Deeper and tense at the dermal-epidermal junction.

optionExplanations.b: Pemphigus vulgaris produces flaccid, non-pruritic intraepidermal bullae with mouth involvement in 90% and a positive Nikolsky sign.
optionExplanations.c: Toxic epidermal necrolysis follows a culprit drug with dusky tender skin, mucosal erosions, and epidermal detachment over more than 30% of body surface area.
optionExplanations.d: Bullous impetigo is an infectious eruption in children with superficial bullae and honey-coloured crusting.
optionExplanations.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis produces grouped intensely pruritic vesicles rather than large tense bullae in these flexural sites.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man has 2 months of painful oral erosions and now flaccid, non-pruritic blisters on the scalp, chest, and axillae that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Lateral pressure on intact skin adjacent to a blister causes the epidermis to shear away. Which investigation finding would best confirm the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Intraepidermal IgG and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence
Linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
Granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae
Multinucleated giant epithelial cells on Tzanck smear
Septate hyphae on potassium hydroxide preparation

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes pemphigus vulgaris as an autoimmune blistering disease of flaccid, non-pruritic intraepidermal bullae on mucous membranes and skin, with the mouth involved in 90% of cases and a positive Nikolsky sign of epidermal detachment with shear stress. Its pathogenesis is IgG directed against epidermal desmoglein-1 and -3, and investigations show intraepidermal IgG and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence plus circulating anti-desmoglein IgG.

optionExplanations.b: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane is the immunofluorescence pattern of bullous pemphigoid, which produces tense subepidermal bullae.
optionExplanations.c: Granular IgA in dermal papillae characterises dermatitis herpetiformis, not pemphigus vulgaris.
optionExplanations.d: A Tzanck smear with multinucleated giant epithelial cells indicates herpes simplex infection.
optionExplanations.e: Hyphae on KOH preparation indicate a dermatophyte infection.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman started allopurinol 2 weeks ago. She now has fever, malaise, and a dusky, tender morbilliform eruption on the face and extremities that has coalesced into flaccid blisters with sheets of skin sloughing over roughly 40% of her body surface area. Her lips, oral mucosa, and conjunctivae are eroded, and shear stress detaches the epidermis. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop allopurinol and admit to a burn or intensive care unit for supportive care
Continue allopurinol and start a potent topical corticosteroid
Start intravenous cloxacillin and manage on a general medical ward
Start oral acyclovir and discharge with follow-up in 48 hours
Start oral doxycycline and daily saline compresses at home

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies toxic epidermal necrolysis as epidermal detachment over more than 30% of body surface area, appearing 1-3 weeks after drug initiation, with allopurinol among the common culprits and mortality of about 30% from fluid loss and infection. Management is to discontinue the offending drug and admit to an intermediate care, intensive care, or burn unit for supportive care including IV fluids, electrolyte replacement, nutritional support, pain control, sterile wound care, and monitoring for infection.

optionExplanations.b: Continuing the culprit drug perpetuates the reaction; withdrawal of the offending drug is the essential first step.
optionExplanations.c: Antistaphylococcal antibiotics do not treat this drug reaction, and the SCORTEN framework directs patients with a score of 2 or more to intensive care or a burn unit.
optionExplanations.d: This is a drug reaction rather than a herpetic infection, and outpatient management is unsafe with 40% epidermal detachment.
optionExplanations.e: Home management with compresses cannot address the fluid loss and infection risk that drive mortality.

source.reference: D26 — Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman presents with 2 days of fever, chills, and a painful facial rash. Examination shows a confluent, bright erythematous, warm plaque over the left cheek that is well demarcated with a sharply raised edge against the surrounding normal skin. She describes the area as burning. There is no fluctuance or necrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes contrasts erysipelas, which involves the upper dermis and presents as a confluent, erythematous, warm plaque that is well demarcated with a sharp raised edge, is very painful (St. Anthony's fire), favours the face and legs, and is caused by group A streptococcus with systemic symptoms of fever, chills, headache and weakness, with cellulitis, which involves the lower dermis and subcutaneous fat and is poorly demarcated and not uniformly raised.

optionExplanations.b: Cellulitis is a poorly demarcated, not uniformly raised, flat erythematous lesion most commonly on the legs.
optionExplanations.c: Contact dermatitis is listed in the differential of cellulitis but is pruritic and eczematous rather than febrile with a sharply raised border.
optionExplanations.d: Superficial folliculitis presents as dome-shaped pustules at the mouths of hair follicles.
optionExplanations.e: A carbuncle is a deep-seated abscess formed by multiple coalescing furuncles draining through several openings.

source.reference: D30 — Bacterial Infections: Dermis / Comparison of Erysipelas and Cellulitis

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has 6 weeks of an itchy scalp with several round scaly patches of alopecia containing broken-off hairs. There is tender occipital lymphadenopathy. KOH preparation of scale and hair shafts shows hyphae, and culture confirms a dermatophyte. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for 4 weeks
Topical mupirocin ointment three times daily for 10 days

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes tinea capitis as round scaly patches of alopecia with broken-off hairs, pruritus, and possible occipital lymphadenopathy, most often in children, and states that oral therapy is indicated for onychomycosis and tinea capitis with terbinafine for 4 weeks. The text explicitly notes that oral agents are required to penetrate the hair root where the dermatophyte resides, with adjunctive antifungal shampoos to limit spread.

optionExplanations.b: Topical azoles are first line for tinea corporis, cruris, and interdigital tinea pedis but cannot reach the dermatophyte in the hair root.
optionExplanations.c: Mupirocin is an antibacterial used for impetigo and superficial folliculitis, not for a dermatophyte.
optionExplanations.d: Intralesional steroids are used for alopecia areata, a non-infectious cause of patchy hair loss.
optionExplanations.e: Minoxidil treats androgenetic alopecia and does not eradicate a fungal infection.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man who worked outdoors for 40 years has a lesion beside his nose that has slowly enlarged over 2 years and occasionally bleeds. Examination shows a 9 mm skin-coloured papule with a rolled, translucent pearly border, fine telangiectasia crossing the surface, and a depressed, eroded centre. There is no lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes nodular basal cell carcinoma, the most common subtype, as a skin-coloured papule or nodule with a rolled, translucent (pearly) telangiectatic border and a depressed, eroded, or ulcerated centre. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in humans, is usually due to UVB exposure with over 80% on sun-exposed sites, and has a latency of 20-50 years between UV damage and onset, which fits this patient's occupational exposure and slow growth.

optionExplanations.b: Squamous cell carcinoma is a hyperkeratotic indurated papule, plaque, or nodule with surface scale or crust that enlarges more rapidly than a basal cell carcinoma.
optionExplanations.c: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing dome-shaped volcano-like nodule with a central keratin-filled crater.
optionExplanations.d: Bowen's disease is a sharply demarcated erythematous patch or thin plaque with scale or crusting, typically 1-3 cm.
optionExplanations.e: Amelanotic melanoma presents as pink or red macules, papules, or nodules without the pearly rolled telangiectatic border.

source.reference: D40 — Nonmelanoma Skin Cancers / Basal Cell Carcinoma

questions.question: A 47-year-old fair-skinned woman with red hair and multiple dysplastic nevi presents with a lesion on her upper back that her partner noticed changing. It is an 11 mm asymmetric plaque with an irregular indistinct border and mixed red, white, and blue-black colouration, and it has become slightly raised over 4 months. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Shave biopsy of the most raised portion
Topical imiquimod 5% cream three times weekly
Photographic surveillance with review in 6 months

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes applies the ABCDE checklist (asymmetry, irregular border, varied colour, diameter over 6 mm, and enlargement or evolution) to identify malignant features of a mole, and describes superficial spreading melanoma as irregular, indurated, enlarging plaques with red, white, and blue discolouration. For management, excisional biopsy is preferable, with the definitive margin determined by Breslow depth and wider excision performed only after histologic diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: A shave biopsy risks transecting the lesion and losing the depth measurement on which staging and margins depend.
optionExplanations.c: Cryotherapy destroys tissue and leaves no specimen for the histologic diagnosis and Breslow depth.
optionExplanations.d: Imiquimod is indicated for superficial basal cell carcinoma, Bowen's disease, actinic keratoses, and warts.
optionExplanations.e: Deferring diagnosis in a lesion with several ABCDE features risks progression, and lesions that regress are often deeper than anticipated.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has a 3-month history of an itchy eruption on both earlobes and on the wrist under her watch strap. Examination shows erythema with a papulovesicular eruption and swelling limited to the areas in contact with her jewellery, with normal surrounding skin. She has no history of atopy. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Potassium hydroxide preparation of skin scrapings
Bacterial swab for culture and sensitivity

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies allergic contact dermatitis as a cell-mediated delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction producing erythema with a papulovesicular eruption, swelling, and pruritus in areas exposed to the allergen, with nickel listed among the common allergens. Patch testing is used to determine the specific allergen so that the allergen and its cross-reactants can be avoided, with topical corticosteroids BID prn for symptoms. This woman's eruption is confined to sites of jewellery contact, which is the pattern of an acquired allergen susceptibility rather than a toxic irritant injury.

optionExplanations.b: A potassium hydroxide preparation looks for a dermatophyte, which does not produce swelling confined to jewellery contact sites.
optionExplanations.c: Direct immunofluorescence is used for immunobullous disease, not for identifying a contact allergen.
optionExplanations.d: A total IgE level does not identify the responsible contact allergen in a delayed type IV reaction.
optionExplanations.e: Bacterial culture is used when secondary infection is suspected, and it will not identify the causative allergen.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man reports 6 months of an itchy, flaky scalp. Examination shows diffuse involvement of the scalp margin with yellow to white flakes and underlying erythema, together with greasy erythematous scaling in the nasolabial folds and eyebrows. There is no hair loss and no nail change. What is the best initial treatment for his scalp?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes adult seborrheic dermatitis as diffuse involvement of the scalp margin with yellow to white flakes, pruritus, and underlying erythema, with additional involvement of the nasolabial folds and eyebrows, and attributes it to Malassezia species. For the scalp, management is ketoconazole 2% shampoo, ciclopirox shampoo, selenium sulfide or zinc pyrithione shampoo, or a steroid lotion. His greasy scaling in sebaceous gland-rich sites fits this diagnosis, so an antifungal shampoo is the appropriate first step.

optionExplanations.b: Oral terbinafine is reserved for onychomycosis and tinea capitis, not for seborrheic dermatitis.
optionExplanations.c: Permethrin treats scabies and pediculosis, neither of which produces greasy scaling of the nasolabial folds.
optionExplanations.d: Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated for localized seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp.
optionExplanations.e: Topical vitamin D analogues are used for psoriasis rather than as first-line therapy for seborrheic dermatitis.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man develops a widespread eruption 2 weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis. Examination shows discrete, scattered, salmon-pink small scaling papules over the trunk and legs, sparing the palms and soles. There is no herald patch, no mucosal lesion, and no lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes guttate psoriasis as discrete, scattered salmon-pink small scaling papules distributed diffusely, usually on the trunk and legs and sparing the palms and soles, with an often antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis. Management is broadband UVB phototherapy, sunlight and emollients, with penicillin V, erythromycin, or azithromycin if group A streptococcus is grown on throat culture. The drop-like papules appearing shortly after pharyngitis in this young man match that description.

optionExplanations.b: Pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch and produces oval plaques following skin tension lines rather than drop-like salmon-pink papules after pharyngitis.
optionExplanations.c: Secondary syphilis characteristically involves the palms and soles and is accompanied by generalized lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms.
optionExplanations.d: Nummular dermatitis produces coin-shaped, dry, scaly, pruritic plaques rather than showers of small scaling papules.
optionExplanations.e: Tinea corporis produces a scaly annular plaque with an active margin, not a diffuse scattered papular eruption.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man has several months of an intensely pruritic, burning eruption. Examination shows grouped papules, vesicles, and urticarial wheals on an erythematous base, bilaterally symmetrical over the extensor elbows and knees, sacrum, and buttocks, with numerous excoriations. Immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows IgA deposits. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes dermatitis herpetiformis as grouped papules, vesicles, and urticarial wheals on an erythematous base with intense pruritus, burning and excoriations, symmetrically distributed on the extensor elbows and knees, sacrum, and buttocks, with immunofluorescence showing IgA deposits in perilesional skin. Management is dapsone, with sulfapyridine if dapsone is contraindicated or poorly tolerated, plus a gluten-free diet for life, which also reduces the risk of intestinal lymphoma in the 90% who have gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

optionExplanations.b: Systemic corticosteroids are not the recommended treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis.
optionExplanations.c: Doxycycline is used for acne, rosacea, and bullous pemphigoid, not for this IgA-mediated eruption.
optionExplanations.d: A potent topical steroid does not address the underlying gluten-sensitive enteropathy or control the eruption.
optionExplanations.e: Despite the name, this is not a herpesvirus infection and antivirals have no role.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy finished a course of cefaclor for otitis media 12 days ago. He now has a symmetrical urticarial cutaneous eruption with low grade fever, malaise, arthralgia, and lymphadenopathy. There is no facial edema, no mucosal involvement, and no bronchospasm. Liver enzymes and eosinophil count are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes a serum sickness-like reaction as a symmetrical cutaneous eruption that is usually urticarial, accompanied by malaise, low grade fever, arthralgia, and lymphadenopathy, appearing 1-3 weeks after drug initiation and resolving 2-3 weeks after withdrawal. It is more prevalent in children, and cefaclor is the common causative agent in children. Management is to discontinue the offending drug with or without topical or oral corticosteroids.

optionExplanations.b: DRESS presents with a morbilliform rash, facial edema, and internal organ involvement such as hepatitis and hematologic abnormalities, which are absent here.
optionExplanations.c: An exanthematous drug reaction produces erythematous macules and papules rather than an urticarial eruption with arthralgia and lymphadenopathy.
optionExplanations.d: Drug-induced urticaria and angioedema involves wheals with swelling of the face and mucous membranes and may be accompanied by anaphylaxis.
optionExplanations.e: Erythema multiforme produces target lesions rather than a symmetrical urticarial eruption with a serum sickness picture.

source.reference: D25 — Drug Eruptions / Serum Sickness-Like Reaction

questions.question: A 24-year-old man has 4 weeks of intense pruritus that is worst at night. Examination shows superficial linear burrows in the finger web spaces and wrists, with inflammatory papules and nodules in the axillae and groin and excoriated crusted papules on the buttocks. The head and neck are spared. His roommate has similar itching. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Permethrin 5% cream applied from the neck down to the soles, left on 8-14 hours, and repeated in 7 days
Clotrimazole cream applied twice daily for 4 weeks
Mid-potency topical corticosteroid twice daily alone

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes characterizes scabies by superficial linear burrows, intense pruritus that is especially nocturnal, and inflammatory papules and nodules in the axilla and groin, affecting the axillae, groin, buttocks, hands and feet, particularly the web spaces, while sparing the head and neck except in infants. Management is to bathe and then apply permethrin 5% cream from the neck down to the soles of the feet, left on for 8-14 h, with a second treatment 7 days later, plus treating family and close contacts and laundering linens.

optionExplanations.b: Topical antifungals treat dermatophyte infection and have no effect on Sarcoptes scabiei.
optionExplanations.c: Oral antibiotics only address secondary bacterial infection and do not eradicate the mite.
optionExplanations.d: Mid-potency topical steroids and antihistamines are for symptom control after permethrin, since pruritus may persist 2-3 weeks after effective treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Systemic steroids do not eradicate the infestation and will not prevent transmission to contacts.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man presents with a genital lesion he noticed 10 days ago. Examination shows a single red, indurated, painless ulcer with a raised border and scanty serous exudate, with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Dark field examination of fluid from the lesion shows spirochetes. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose
Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks
Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 14 days
Valacyclovir 1 g PO twice daily for 3 days

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes primary syphilis as a single red, indurated, painless chancre developing into a painless ulcer with a raised border and scanty serous exudate at the site of inoculation, with regional non-tender lymphadenopathy appearing less than a week after onset, and dark field examination showing the spirochete in chancre fluid. Treatment of primary syphilis is penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose.

optionExplanations.b: Weekly penicillin G for 3 weeks is the regimen listed for tertiary syphilis, which occurs 3-7 years after the secondary stage.
optionExplanations.c: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV every 24 h is the treatment listed for disseminated gonococcal infection, which causes hemorrhagic tender pustules on a purpuric background.
optionExplanations.d: Doxycycline is not the regimen Toronto Notes gives for primary syphilis.
optionExplanations.e: Antivirals treat herpes simplex, which produces multiple painful lesions rather than a single painless indurated chancre.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with a lifetime of heavy sun exposure describes several rough spots on his hairless scalp and on the helices of both ears. Examination shows ill-defined, scaly, erythematous papules with white to yellow scale on sun-damaged skin. They are easier to appreciate on palpation than on inspection, with a gritty, sandpaper-like texture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes actinic keratoses as ill-defined, scaly, erythematous papules or plaques on sun-damaged skin, with an initial rough erythematous papule bearing white to yellow scale that is often easier to appreciate on palpation than inspection because of its gritty, sandpaper-like texture, on sites of sun exposure such as the hairless scalp and helices of the ears in men. Risk of transformation to SCC is under 1 in 1000 per year but is higher if the lesion persists.

optionExplanations.b: Seborrheic keratoses are a listed differential but are stuck-on waxy lesions rather than gritty scaly papules on sun-damaged skin.
optionExplanations.c: Superficial basal cell carcinoma is in the differential but presents as a discrete lesion rather than multiple gritty rough papules across chronically sun-exposed skin.
optionExplanations.d: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ presents as a sharply demarcated erythematous patch or thin plaque with scale or crusting, typically 1-3 cm.
optionExplanations.e: Discoid lupus produces erythematous plaques with keratotic scale, follicular plugging, and atrophic scarring.

source.reference: D39 — Pre-Malignant Skin Conditions / Actinic Keratoses

questions.question: A 68-year-old renal transplant recipient reports a lesion on the helix of his right ear that has enlarged over 3 months. Examination shows a 1.5 cm hyperkeratotic, indurated, pink papule and plaque with surface scale and crust and early ulceration, growing outward. It has enlarged much faster than a previous lesion excised from his cheek. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma as a hyperkeratotic indurated pink, red, or skin-coloured papule, plaque, or nodule with surface scale or crust and possible ulceration, enlarging more rapidly than BCC and growing exophytically, on sites such as the face, ears, scalp, forearms, and dorsum of the hands. SCC is the most common cutaneous malignancy in immunocompromised patients such as organ transplant recipients, with increased mortality compared with the non-immunocompromised population.

optionExplanations.b: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing dome-shaped volcano-like nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, which is not described here.
optionExplanations.c: Bowen's disease is a sharply demarcated erythematous patch or thin plaque with scale, without induration or exophytic growth.
optionExplanations.d: A hypertrophic actinic keratosis is a thicker rough papule or plaque, but it is pre-malignant and does not ulcerate or grow rapidly.
optionExplanations.e: Basal cell carcinoma enlarges more slowly than SCC and does not typically produce a hyperkeratotic crusted surface.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman has noticed two round patches of complete hair loss on her scalp over 6 weeks. The underlying skin is smooth and non-scaly with no erythema or pustules. At the margins there are short hairs with tapered fractured shafts resembling exclamation marks. Her fingernails show fine stippling and pitting. She has autoimmune thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes alopecia areata as an autoimmune disorder with patches of complete hair loss, often localized to the scalp, that may be associated with dystrophic nail changes of fine stippling and pitting and with an exclamation mark pattern in which hairs are fractured with tapered shafts. It may be associated with other autoimmune conditions including thyroid disease, pernicious anemia, vitiligo, and Addison's disease, and localized disease carries an excellent prognosis with topical or intralesional steroids.

optionExplanations.b: Telogen effluvium produces a uniform decrease in hair density after a precipitant rather than discrete patches of complete loss.
optionExplanations.c: Trichotillomania produces irregular patches with remaining hairs broken at varying lengths from compulsive pulling.
optionExplanations.d: Androgenetic alopecia in women causes widening of the central part in a Christmas tree pattern, not discrete round bald patches.
optionExplanations.e: Anagen effluvium follows chemotherapy or other agents that impair mitotic activity of the follicle and causes diffuse loss.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman is assessed for several months of fatigue. Examination of her nails shows bilateral spoon shaped nails affecting several fingers. There is no pitting, no onycholysis, no clubbing, and no nail fold change. The nail plates are otherwise intact and the skin examination is normal. Which underlying condition is most likely associated with this nail finding?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines koilonychia as spoon shaped nails and lists its associated diseases as iron deficiency, malnutrition, and diabetes mellitus. Nail plate changes are a useful marker of systemic disease, and in a fatigued patient with spoon shaped nails and no other nail plate or surface abnormality, iron deficiency is the association to pursue.

optionExplanations.b: Psoriasis is associated with pitting in a random pattern, onycholysis, and oil spots rather than koilonychia.
optionExplanations.c: Thyroid disease is listed as a cause of onycholysis, which is separation of the nail plate from the nail bed.
optionExplanations.d: Cyanotic heart disease is associated with clubbing, in which the proximal nail plate has greater than a 180 degree angle to the nail fold.
optionExplanations.e: Scleroderma is associated with pterygium inversum unguis and nail fold telangiectasias.

source.reference: D46 — Nails and Disorders of the Nail Apparatus

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman has 1 week of painful lumps on her shins with arthralgia, low grade fever, and malaise. Examination shows round, red, tender, poorly demarcated nodules asymmetrically arranged over both extensor lower legs, with no ulceration and no overlying blister. She takes no medications and has had no diarrhea. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Venous duplex ultrasound of the legs

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes erythema nodosum as an acute or chronic inflammation of subcutaneous fat producing round, red, tender, poorly demarcated nodules arranged asymmetrically on the extensor lower legs, associated with arthralgia, fever, and malaise. Investigations are a chest x-ray to rule out chest infection and sarcoidosis, plus throat culture, ASO titre, and PPD skin test. Because 40% are idiopathic and the remainder reflect an underlying cause such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or streptococcal infection, imaging the chest is the key first step while the lesions resolve spontaneously over about 6 weeks.

optionExplanations.b: Duplex ultrasound assesses venous thrombosis, which does not produce multiple tender nodules on both shins.
optionExplanations.c: Erythema nodosum is a clinical diagnosis, and biopsy does not identify the underlying systemic cause.
optionExplanations.d: An antinuclear antibody is not among the listed investigations for erythema nodosum.
optionExplanations.e: Blood cultures are not part of the recommended workup for this panniculitis.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman has a mild eczematous dermatitis affecting both cheeks and both axillae. Emollients alone have not controlled it and she now needs a topical corticosteroid. She is worried about long term thinning of the skin and visible blood vessels at the treated sites. Which topical corticosteroid is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes ranks weak topical steroids such as hydrocortisone for use on intertriginous areas, in children, and on the face and thin skin, while the very potent and extremely potent agents are listed for the palms and soles. Relative percutaneous absorption is much higher on the cheeks than the forearm, so potency must be reduced at these sites. Local side effects of topical steroids include atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, perioral dermatitis, and hypopigmentation, which is precisely what this patient wishes to avoid on the face and axillae.

optionExplanations.b: Hydrocortisone 17-valerate is a moderate potency steroid listed for the arm, leg, and trunk rather than the face or flexures.
optionExplanations.c: Betamethasone 17-valerate 0.1% is a potent steroid listed for the body and scalp and risks atrophy on facial and intertriginous skin.
optionExplanations.d: Fluocinonide 0.05% is a very potent agent listed for the palms and soles.
optionExplanations.e: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% is the most potent topical steroid and is reserved for palms and soles.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with stable congestive heart failure has thickened, crumbling, discoloured toenails and requests oral treatment. The diagnosis of onychomycosis has been confirmed before treatment. He has no liver disease, normal renal function, and takes no statin, beta-blocker, or antiarrhythmic agent. Topical therapy has already failed. Which oral therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Terbinafine 250 mg PO once daily for 12 weeks
Itraconazole 200 mg PO twice daily for 3 days each month, repeated 3 times

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists terbinafine 250 mg PO once daily for onychomycosis, given for 12 weeks for toenails and 6 weeks for fingernails, with the diagnosis confirmed prior to treatment; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in chronic or active liver disease, and it concentrates rapidly in skin, hair, and nails at fungicidal levels. Itraconazole is the alternative oral agent for onychomycosis but is contraindicated in congestive heart failure and carries serious hepatotoxicity, which makes terbinafine the appropriate choice in this man.

optionExplanations.b: Itraconazole is listed as contraindicated in CHF and carries a risk of serious hepatotoxicity and CYP3A4 inhibition.
optionExplanations.c: Doxycycline is indicated for acne vulgaris, rosacea, and bullous pemphigoid, not for a fungal nail infection.
optionExplanations.d: Dapsone is used for dermatitis herpetiformis and neutrophilic dermatoses and has no antifungal activity.
optionExplanations.e: Acitretin is used for severe psoriasis and disorders of hyperkeratinization such as ichthyosis.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman describes 3 years of recurrent painful nodules in both axillae and the inguinal folds. She smokes and has gained considerable weight since her teens. Examination shows inflammatory nodules with sinus formation, clusters of open comedones, and hypertrophic scarring of the intertriginous areas, with marked hyperpigmentation. She has no diarrhea, weight loss, or perianal fistula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines hidradenitis suppurativa as a chronic scarring inflammatory skin condition resulting from follicular occlusion and inflammation within intertriginous zones and areas rich in apocrine glands. The primary lesions are inflammatory nodules, with sinus formation, clusters of open comedones, and hypertrophic scarring of intertriginous areas, most commonly the axillae followed by the inguinal area and inner thighs. Onset between puberty and age 40, female predominance, significant hyperpigmentation in more pigmented skin, and associations with smoking and excess weight all fit this patient, and the diagnosis is clinical.

optionExplanations.a: Folliculitis is listed in the differential but produces superficial follicular pustules rather than sinus tracts, double tombstone comedones, and hypertrophic scarring of intertriginous skin.
optionExplanations.b: Acne vulgaris affects sebaceous areas such as the face, chest, and back rather than the axillae and inguinal folds, and does not form draining sinus tracts.
optionExplanations.d: Crohn's disease is in the differential of hidradenitis suppurativa, but she has no diarrhea, weight loss, or perianal fistula to suggest bowel involvement.
optionExplanations.e: Recurrent pilonidal sinus is confined to the natal cleft; it does not explain bilateral axillary and inguinal nodules, although pilonidal disease can accompany hidradenitis as part of the follicular occlusion tetrad.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man has recurrent attacks of deep swelling of the lips, tongue, and hands since childhood, each lasting about 2 days. Episodes follow minor trauma, emotional upset, or temperature changes. The swelling is never accompanied by pruritic wheals and does not respond to antihistamines. He takes no medications. His father and sister have identical attacks, and an uncle died of laryngeal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Non-allergic drug reaction to an ACE inhibitor

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes angioedema as deeper swelling of the skin involving subcutaneous tissues, often the eyes, lips, and tongue, which may or may not accompany urticaria. The hereditary form does not occur with urticaria, has onset in childhood with a positive family history in 80%, produces recurrent attacks triggered by minor trauma, emotional upset, or temperature changes, and kills 25% of patients through laryngeal edema. Childhood onset, absence of wheals, characteristic triggers, and affected first-degree relatives make hereditary angioedema the diagnosis; prophylaxis is with danazol or stanozolol, with an epinephrine pen to temporize until the patient reaches hospital in an acute attack.

optionExplanations.a: Acute allergic angioedema is an acquired form triggered by an identifiable allergen such as food, drugs, contrast media, insect venom, or latex, not by minor trauma or temperature change, and it does not run in families.
optionExplanations.c: A non-allergic drug reaction to an ACE inhibitor is an acquired cause of angioedema, but this man takes no medications.
optionExplanations.d: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency is also an acquired form, so it would not explain onset in childhood with affected first-degree relatives.
optionExplanations.e: Urticaria consists of transient, red, pruritic, well-demarcated wheals with each individual lesion lasting less than 24 h, and antihistamines are first line for symptomatic relief; this man has deep swelling without wheals.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman reports 6 months of a painful lesion on the dorsolateral aspect of her right fifth toe that hurts with direct pressure from her shoes. Examination shows a firm papule with a central, translucent, cone-shaped, hard keratin core. Paring produces no bleeding and no black speckling, and the epidermal ridge pattern is interrupted over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Corns are described as a firm papule with a central, translucent, cone-shaped, hard keratin core that is painful with direct pressure and interrupts dermatoglyphics, arising from localized hyperkeratosis induced by pressure and most commonly found on the dorsolateral fifth toe. The paring test separates the differential: warts bleed with paring and show a black speckled centre from thrombosed capillaries, while calluses reveal layers of yellowish keratin with no thrombosed capillaries and no interruption of epidermal ridges. This lesion's keratin core, pressure-related pain, absence of bleeding on paring, and interrupted dermatoglyphics identify a corn.

optionExplanations.b: A callus shows layers of yellowish keratin on paring with no central translucent core and no interruption of the epidermal ridges.
optionExplanations.c: A plantar wart bleeds with paring and has a black speckled central appearance from thrombosed capillaries; it destroys rather than merely interrupts dermatoglyphics.
optionExplanations.d: Actinic keratoses (solar keratoses) are pre-malignant lesions of chronically sun-exposed skin, not a pressure-induced hyperkeratotic papule with a translucent keratin core on a toe.
optionExplanations.e: Keloids are firm, shiny, skin-coloured or red-bluish papules or nodules that follow cutaneous injury and extend beyond the original margins with claw-like extensions, typically on earlobes, shoulders, sternum, scapular area, or angle of the mandible.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man describes 4 years of visible, excessive sweating of both palms, both soles, and both axillae that soaks his shirts and smudges his written work. The sweating occurs only during waking hours and never disturbs his sleep. He takes no medications and has no other symptoms. His father and sister are similarly affected. Examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Autonomic dysreflexia from spinal cord injury

questions.explanation: Primary hyperhidrosis is secretion of sweat in amounts greater than physiologically needed for thermoregulation, defined as focal, visible, excessive sweating of at least 6 months without apparent cause, developing in childhood or adolescence and persisting through life. It is diurnal, occurring only during waking hours, is typically localized to the palms, soles, and axillae, and most patients have a family history. This young man meets every one of those descriptors and none of the listed secondary causes applies, so the diagnosis is clinical.

optionExplanations.b: Medications such as antidepressants, antipyretics, cholinergic agonists, and hormonal agents are listed causes of secondary sweating, but he takes no medications.
optionExplanations.c: Excessive heat is an environmental cause on the differential; his sweating is focal, lifelong, and unrelated to ambient temperature.
optionExplanations.d: Spinal cord injury with autonomic dysreflexia is a secondary cause, but he has no injury history and his examination is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Post-traumatic syringomyelia is another spinal cord injury complication on the differential and again requires antecedent trauma, which is absent here.
